title: The years and the days
hook: the years teach much which the days never know (Experience)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was grief that teaches nothing: Emerson refusing to turn his son's death into a lesson. Your line was it taught nothing.

An old photo turns up, taken about this time last year. A kitchen, a face, a sky. Where was that, again? What was going on that week? The particular day is mostly gone. But the year it belonged to has a shape now that it didn't have then: what started, what ended, what turned out to matter and what didn't. Emerson put that difference into one plain sentence, in the same essay as yesterday's grief.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM LAST YEAR.` → `THE DAY IS GONE.` → `THE YEAR HAS A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: First, the line, from Experience: "The years teach much which the days never know." The years teach. The days never know. Second, why the days can't know. A single day is too close to see. Inside it you're answering messages, making dinner, worrying about a meeting. You can see the weather, not the climate. A choice that will change everything can look, on the day, like a small errand: a phone call returned, a class signed up for, a door knocked on. Nothing in that day announces what it is. Third, why the years can. Distance does what closeness can't. From a year or more away, the scattered days take on a shape. The worry that filled a whole month shrinks to a footnote, and a quiet habit you barely noticed turns out to have carried you. That knowledge isn't available on the day; it has to be waited for. Fourth, how it sits beside yesterday. Yesterday Emerson said his grief taught him nothing. Today, from the same essay, the years teach much. He doesn't tie the two together, and it would be wrong to say he does. But a reader can hold both: a day of loss may teach nothing at all, and it doesn't have to. Whatever the years teach, they teach slowly. The gift in that is patience. Today doesn't have to make sense today.
screen: `THE YEARS TEACH MUCH.` · `A DAY IS TOO CLOSE TO SEE.` · `DISTANCE GIVES THE DAYS A SHAPE.` · `THE SAME ESSAY AS YESTERDAY.` · then, large: `THE DAYS NEVER KNOW.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go back to about this time last year: where you were living, what worried you, who was close. Come forward slowly, season by season, without judging any of it. Notice one thing that looked small then and turned out to matter, or one worry that turned out smaller than it seemed.

howItsDone: Readers often reach for this line from Emerson's Experience at birthdays, new years and anniversaries, as a reminder that some things can only be understood from a distance.
